title: There are moments when heaven feels too quiet.
paragraphs: There are moments when heaven feels too quiet.
Moments when the command of God sounds so sharp, so costly, that your whole soul trembles under its weight.

Genesis 22 opens on a mountain road, with wood on a son’s back, fire in a father’s hand, and a word from God that no parent would ever want to hear: “Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest… and offer him” (Genesis 22:2). The scene is holy, but it feels unbearable. Morning light. Dust on sandals. A knife hidden in obedience. Abraham walks forward, not because the path makes sense, but because the God who spoke had never failed him before.
This is where many believers go silent.

Because we do not mind promises. We struggle with surrender. We celebrate Genesis 21 moments when Isaac is born, but we tremble in Genesis 22 when God touches the very blessing He gave. And sometimes that is exactly how the test comes—not through what is evil, but through what is precious.
Pause.

The test was never because God was cruel. Scripture is clear: “God did tempt Abraham” in the older KJV language, meaning He tested him, not enticed him to sin (Genesis 22:1; James 1:13). The Lord was revealing what sat highest on Abraham’s altar. Some scholars interpret this passage as the supreme proving of covenant faith. Others emphasize that it exposes the heart’s tendency to cling even to God-given gifts more tightly than to God Himself. Either way, the question burns: when blessing and obedience seem to collide, whom will you trust?
That question still reaches us.

Not on Mount Moriah with literal fire and wood, but in hospital corridors, empty wallets, delayed answers, broken engagements, prodigal children, and prayers that seem to rise and fall back unanswered. God tests faith where it hurts. He presses where idols hide. He calls where comfort protests. Holy versus broken. Silence versus voice. Calling versus craving.

And here is the mid-story ache: Isaac was not just Abraham’s son. Isaac was the promise. Through Isaac would come descendants, covenant, future (Genesis 17:19). So when Abraham obeyed, he was not merely risking loss. He was placing God’s own promise back into God’s own hands. He ran… but not away. He walked uphill into the wound, believing that if God required everything, God could still remain faithful.

Hebrews 11:19 gives us a window into Abraham’s faith: he believed God could raise Isaac from the dead. Think about that. Before resurrection was a doctrine fully unfolded, Abraham trusted the character of God beyond what he could see. That is mountain faith. Not loud faith. Not polished faith. Faith with tears in its throat and obedience in its feet.
Then comes the turn.

Just as the knife is lifted, heaven speaks: “Lay not thine hand upon the lad” (Genesis 22:12). And there, caught in a thicket, is a ram provided by God. Abraham names the place Jehovah-jireh, “The Lord will provide” (Genesis 22:14). Do not miss this: God did not desire Isaac’s blood. He desired Abraham’s trust. The son was spared. The substitute was given.
Here the story opens wider than Moriah.

Genesis 22 whispers the Gospel before Calvary shouts it. Isaac carried wood; Jesus carried the cross. Isaac was spared; Jesus was not spared. Abraham received a ram in place of his son; we receive Christ, the true Lamb of God, in place of us. This is the blazing center: your hardest test is not proof that God has abandoned you. For those in Christ, it may be the place where God strips away false securities so you can see the greater provision—Jesus alone.

So when God tests you, do not assume He is destroying you. He may be uncovering what owns you. He may be teaching you that the promise is never safer in your hands than in His. To the brother hiding his panic behind a strong face, to the weary mother crying in secret, to the friend who stopped praying because the wait became too heavy—look again at Moriah. The same God who tests is the God who provides.
And when this hits again, remember this line: what God asks for, He is able to guard; what God seems to delay, He is still able to redeem.
Many have found that the deeper discipleship begins right there, where surrender stops being poetic and becomes personal.
You are not alone on the mountain. And if Jesus is your Savior, the fire of testing will never outshine the mercy of the God who already gave His Son for you.
Stand firm, Gospel Warrior.
